mcqs.question: The detection algorithm reduces the resource allocation graph and finds that P1, P2, and P3 can all be marked as able to finish, but P4 and P5 cannot, no matter what order is tried. What does this mean?
options: P4 and P5 are in an actual, confirmed deadlock right now
The system made an error and should retry the algorithm
P4 and P5 are merely in an unsafe state, not an actual deadlock
P1, P2, and P3 are the ones deadlocked, since they were processed first
mcqs.explanation: Processes that can never be marked finishable, no matter how the reduction proceeds, are exactly the ones involved in a real, currently-occurring deadlock — detection confirms actual deadlock, unlike avoidance's 'unsafe' which is only a risk. Processes that do reduce successfully are not deadlocked; there's no error to retry.

mcqs.question: Why don't systems that use detection-and-recovery simply run the detection algorithm after every single resource request, to catch deadlocks as fast as possible?
options: Running it that frequently would recreate a cost similar to avoidance's per-request overhead, undermining the whole point of paying nothing on the common path
The algorithm can only be run once per day for correctness reasons
It would make deadlocks impossible to detect at all
Running it more often always makes the system slower with no other trade-off to consider
mcqs.explanation: Detection-and-recovery's appeal is near-zero cost on the common, non-deadlocking path; running detection on every request reintroduces a per-request cost similar to avoidance, defeating that advantage. It's a real trade-off (frequency vs. how long a deadlock might sit undetected), not a correctness or detectability issue.

mcqs.question: Why can databases use resource preemption (rolling back a transaction) as deadlock recovery, when a general-purpose OS usually can't do the equivalent for arbitrary processes holding arbitrary resources?
options: Because database transactions are already built to be rollback-safe by design, so undoing one cleanly is a well-defined, already-existing operation — most general resources and processes have no equivalent clean undo
Because databases never actually experience deadlocks in practice
Because database transactions run faster than OS processes, making rollback free
Because rolling back a transaction requires no special support from the database engine
mcqs.explanation: Rollback is only a viable recovery mechanism because it's a first-class, safe operation transactions are specifically designed to support (part of atomicity) — most arbitrary OS resources (a printer mid-print, an in-progress external side effect) have no equivalent clean way to undo. Databases do experience deadlocks regularly; rollback requires real engine support, it isn't free.

mcqs.question: A database's deadlock victim selection always picks the transaction with the lowest priority. What long-term problem can this cause for one specific low-priority, frequently-conflicting transaction?
options: It will be granted extra resources to compensate
Nothing — priority-based selection has no downside
It could be repeatedly chosen as the victim every time it deadlocks, and never actually complete — a form of starvation caused by the recovery mechanism itself
The database will automatically raise its priority after one rollback
mcqs.explanation: Always picking the same criterion for victim selection can cause one process to be selected repeatedly, preventing it from ever finishing — starvation introduced by the recovery strategy, not the scheduler. Real systems fix this by factoring in rollback history so a repeatedly-chosen victim becomes progressively less likely to be picked again; this isn't automatic without such a fix.

mcqs.question: Which of the three deadlock-handling strategies pays essentially zero cost on the common, non-deadlocking path, at the cost of allowing deadlock to actually occur sometimes?
options: Detection and recovery
Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm)
Prevention via acquiring all resources upfront
All three pay the same cost regardless of approach
mcqs.explanation: Detection and recovery's defining trade is near-zero common-path cost in exchange for allowing real deadlocks to occasionally happen before reacting. Avoidance pays a real safety-check cost on every request; upfront-acquisition prevention pays a utilization cost by holding resources early. The three strategies have clearly different cost profiles.
